advisor.summary: Holding the business's building outside the operating entity and leasing it back at market rent is the cleanest character conversion in the library: OpCo deducts the rent under §162, and the owner's rental income stays out of self-employment income under §1402(a)(1) — dollars that would have surfaced as SE-taxed profit arrive carrying income tax only. The governing constraint is the self-rental rule of Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6): net rental income from a tenant business in which the taxpayer materially participates is recharacterized as nonpassive and can never absorb passive losses, while net losses on the same property stay passive and can strand. Krukowski and Fransen closed the courthouse door on attacking the rule, so the remaining work is planning: set rent from real comparables, choose deliberately between living with the asymmetry and making the sticky Reg. §1.469-4 grouping election, and sequence any cost segregation study after that choice, not before. For S corporation owners the SE-tax benefit is smaller — distributions already avoid it — and the case rests on liability isolation, exit flexibility, and QBI placement.
mechanics: The structure: the owner (or a dedicated LLC) holds the building; the operating entity leases it under a written market-rate lease and deducts the rent under §162(a)(3), while the owner reports the rental on Schedule E.

The character conversion runs through §1402(a)(1): real estate rentals are excluded from self-employment income, so rent that replaces sole-proprietor or general-partner profit sidesteps the 15.3%/2.9%/0.9% stack — while for S corporation owners, whose distributions already escape SE tax, the value shifts to liability isolation and exit design.

Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6) recharacterizes net rental income from a materially participating tenant business as nonpassive — the 'passive income generator' play fails against one's own building — and the asymmetry is deliberate: net losses stay passive under §469, releasing only against passive income or on full disposition under §469(g).

The standard mitigation is the Reg. §1.469-4(d)(1) grouping election, which treats the rental and the operating business as one economic unit where ownership is proportionate; once grouped, depreciation-driven losses are not trapped — but the election is disclosed, binding, and changes how dispositions are tested, so model it before making it.

The rent keeps QBI character: rental to a commonly controlled trade or business is treated as a §199A trade or business under Reg. §1.199A-1(b)(14), with Reg. §1.199A-4 aggregation available when the wage and UBIA limits bind.

Market rent is the non-negotiable foundation: an appraisal or comparable leases in the file, normal terms, actual monthly payment — above-market rent invites reallocation and constructive-dividend exposure; below-market wastes the conversion.

authority.note: The operating entity’s rent deduction — a genuine lease, a reasonable amount, and property the payor does not own.
Excludes real estate rentals from self-employment income — the character conversion at the strategy’s core.
The self-rental recharacterization — net rental income from a materially participating tenant is nonpassive; losses remain passive.
Sustained the recharacterization rule — an attorney’s rental income from his own firm held nonpassive; the leading authority that the rule cannot be litigated away.

authority.cite: Fransen v. United States, 191 F.3d 599 (5th Cir. 1999)
authority.note: Companion appellate validation of the regulation — two circuits, one answer.
The grouping election — rental and operating activity treated as one economic unit — the standard fix for trapped self-rental losses.
Treats a common-control self-rental as a §199A trade or business, preserving QBI on the rent.
Releases suspended passive losses in full on a fully taxable disposition — the eventual exit valve.

requirements: A separate operating entity as tenant, with the real estate titled personally or in its own LLC — never inside the operating company.
A written lease at documented market rent, backed by an appraisal or comparable leases and actually invoiced and paid monthly.
Separate books, bank account, and insurance for the rental — both the liability shield and the tax character depend on real separateness.
A deliberate §469 posture chosen up front: accept the recharacterization asymmetry, or make the grouping election with its disclosure statement.
risks: The leading trap is planning to net self-rental income against passive losses: Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6) forecloses it, and Krukowski v. Commissioner, 279 F.3d 547 (7th Cir. 2002), together with Fransen, makes the rule effectively unchallengeable — any plan that needs self-rental income to be passive is dead on arrival.

Loss stranding is the quieter failure: cost segregation or heavy financing can push the rental negative, and ungrouped losses sit passive — settle the grouping decision before commissioning the study, because the election cannot be retrofitted gracefully.
The grouping election is sticky: it binds future years and changes disposition testing, so a casual election trades one trap for another.
Non-market rent is the exam wedge — above-market invites reallocation and constructive-dividend treatment with a C corporation tenant; there is no safe harbor, only the comparables file.
Moving a building out of an existing corporation is a taxable event; the structure belongs at acquisition, or after a written tax-cost analysis — never as a casual deed transfer.
stateNotes: Conformity: Missouri conforms to the federal passive-activity and SE characterizations through its federal-AGI starting point, so the recharacterization, grouping, and exclusion results flow into the Missouri return unchanged.

PTET interaction: rent shifts income from the operating entity to the rental owner, shrinking the base of an OpCo pass-through entity tax election — and a multi-member rental LLC can make its own Missouri SALT Parity election (RSMo §143.436) — so re-run PTET placement whenever the rent level changes.

Missouri: no state real estate transfer tax applies to deeding the building into the rental LLC, which makes a Missouri retrofit-at-acquisition unusually cheap; lender consent and insurance re-titling remain the practical hurdles.
reviewChecklist: Market-rent support (appraisal or two-plus comparable leases) current and on file; lease executed on normal terms with an actual payment history.
§469 posture documented: asymmetry accepted, or the grouping election attached for the first grouped year with the modeling that justified it.
Any cost segregation study sequenced after the grouping decision.
Rental maintains separate books, banking, and insurance; the tenant entity is real and materially participated in.
QBI treatment and aggregation reviewed wherever the §199A limits bind.
No building moved out of a corporation without a written tax-cost analysis.

client.teaser: Own the building yourself and rent it to your business — same dollars, lighter tax, stronger protection.
client.headline: Become your business's landlord
plainEnglish: Your business needs a home, and someone will collect rent on it. That someone might as well be you. You own the building in your own name or in a simple company, and you lease it to your business at the going rate.

The rent is a normal deductible expense for the business. On your side, the rental income skips the extra 15% self-employment tax that business profit carries. The building also sits outside the business, so a lawsuit against the company cannot reach it.

There is one wrinkle we manage closely. Special IRS rules control how rent income and losses from your own building mix with the rest of your taxes. Courts have tested these rules, and they hold. So we make the setup choices with care on day one — that is much easier than fixing them later.
client.analogy: The rent check your business was always going to write simply gets written to you — and it arrives with less tax taken out than a paycheck or profit draw would.
benefits: Rent reaches you without the extra self-employment tax on business profit
Your building stays shielded from business lawsuits and debts
Keep the building and its rent even if you someday sell the business
Works cleanly alongside depreciation strategies on the property
steps: WE structure the ownership before, or as, you buy the property.
WE document a fair market rent and put a real lease in place.
WE make the technical elections that keep your deductions usable.
YOU pay rent monthly from the business account and keep the two sets of books separate.
clientCommitments: Charge the market rent we document — never a number picked to shift profit around
Keep the rental's money, records, and insurance separate from the business
Check with us before refinancing, big renovations, or a cost segregation study

annualMaintenance: Refresh market-rent comparables and renew the lease each year
Track the rental's income/loss position against the chosen §469 posture
Verify separateness: accounts, books, insurance, and payment history
Re-run PTET placement when rent levels or entity income shift
deliverables: Market-rent support file with the executed lease
Grouping-election analysis and disclosure statement (where elected)

suggest.reason: Owning the building personally and renting to the business needs the self-rental rules managed.
